comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C4, C20, C33-C37 regarding robustness to stochasticity. Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the comparison with oscillating mechanisms and parameter region similarity, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the demonstration of robustness to demographic stochasticity.

Perfect agreement on claims C5, C21, C38-C43 regarding comparison with classical experiments. Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes some speculation about variance sources (C43), while peer reviewers praise the comparison and suggest future work to quantify interference dynamics.

Perfect agreement on claims C15-C18, C63-C65 regarding Beddington-DeAngelis model issues and resolution. Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the theoretical clarification is significant, while peer reviewers acknowledge this as part of the effort to rigorously derive interaction rates.

Disagreement on claim C66 regarding broad applicability. OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED based on successful application across multiple ecosystems. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, noting that the chasing-pair formulation may not hold for many predator-prey systems, potentially limiting generality.

Strong agreement on claims C6, C22, C54-C58 regarding rank-abundance curve matching. Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides quantitative K-S test details, while peer reviewers emphasize the impressive nature of this application. Peer result R4 also includes claims C59-C62 about rare species discrepancy, which OpenEval addresses separately in R8.

Both address the core mechanism of intraspecific interference enabling coexistence. OpenEval R2 focuses on claims C27-C32 (mathematical progression from unstable to stable coexistence), while peer R1 emphasizes claims C3, C19, C29-C32 (the negative feedback mechanism). Both find evidence SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers providing strong affirmation from all three reviewers.

Both address analytical-numerical agreement. OpenEval R3 focuses on claims C3, C19, C49-C50 regarding the core mechanistic finding and analytical predictions matching simulations. Peer R5 addresses claims C49-C50 specifically, affirming technical soundness and rigor of analytical solutions. Both find evidence SUPPORTED.

Both address foundational ecological principles. OpenEval R1 covers claims C1, C2, C10-C12 (competitive exclusion and paradox of plankton), while peer R9 covers broader background claims C1, C2, C7-C14. Both find these established knowledge claims SUPPORTED without challenge.

Both address baseline scenarios without intraspecific interference. OpenEval R2 includes claims C27-C28 as part of the mathematical progression, while peer R6 focuses specifically on these claims showing unstable coexistence. Both find evidence SUPPORTED, establishing the baseline for the main finding.

Both address the rare species discrepancy. OpenEval R8 focuses on claims C59-C62 and rates the explanation as UNCERTAIN due to lack of rigorous testing. Peer R4 includes these claims within a broader SUPPORTED evaluation of rank-abundance curves, acknowledging the discrepancy but accepting the sampling effect explanation.

Both address background ecological knowledge. OpenEval R11 covers claims C7-C9, C13-C14, C67-C69 (prior explanations and their limitations), while peer R9 includes these within broader foundational concepts C1, C2, C7-C14. Both find evidence SUPPORTED as established context.

Both address supporting methodological claims. OpenEval R11 includes claims C67-C69 about prior explanations, while peer R10 covers C67-C69, C75 regarding methodological choices. Both find evidence SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers accepting the theory-driven approach as sufficient.

Both address claim C75 regarding parameter selection methodology. OpenEval R10 finds the approach SUPPORTED but notes the coefficient of variation choice could be better justified. Peer R10 also finds this SUPPORTED, accepting the methodological choices for a theory-driven manuscript.

Both address high-diversity coexistence. OpenEval R6 focuses specifically on claim C46 (many species persisting when Sc >> Sr), while peer R4 includes C46 within broader rank-abundance curve validation (C6, C22, C46, C54-C62). Both find evidence SUPPORTED for the high-diversity finding.

Both address the core negative feedback mechanism. OpenEval R3 focuses on claims C3, C19, C49-C50 (mechanistic finding and analytical-numerical agreement), while peer R1 emphasizes C3, C19, C29-C32 (negative feedback enabling coexistence). Both find evidence SUPPORTED with strong affirmation.
